extracted.intended_audience: newspaper readers and journalists covering wartime military operations
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting on military operations and related political/strategic developments during World War II for a general newspaper audience; combines battlefield dispatches, official statements, enemy broadcasts, and strategic commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source attribution and attribution precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute facts to named official sources, communiqués, or recorded broadcasts (e.g., "Mr. Stimson told his press confer[ence]", "the Navy communique noted", "a Domei news agency reporter’s delayed account", "broadcast picked up ... by the Associated Press listening post").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear attribution for each assertion of fact: name the official (Stimson, Knox), the issuing body (Navy communique), or the provenance of a broadcast (Domei, Tokio radio, AP listening post). When using enemy radio reports or delayed agency accounts, explicitly state how the item was received (picked up, recorded) so readers may judge reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish confirmed facts from unsubstantiated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark enemy or other claims as unsubstantiated when they lack independent confirmation (e.g., "also advanced unsubstantiated claims that heavy losses were inflicted on the Americans").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report claimed figures or dramatic enemy accounts but flag them as unverified. Provide counter-evidence or official statements when available (e.g., Secretary Knox saying American losses lighter than expected) and explain that some broadcasts may be propaganda or later disproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide concrete operational specifics (who, what, where, when, how)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include precise locations, dates, unit names/commanders, tactical maneuvers and sequences (e.g., "landings near the west arm of Holtz Bay", "another landing ... at Massacre Bay", "Major-Gen. Eugene Landrum ... commands the troops", "pincer drive").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the geographic points (Holtz Bay, Massacre Bay, Chichagof Harbor), unit/leader names (Col. Frank L. Culin Jr.), times/dates (May 12, May 14) and describe maneuvers (landings, naval bombardment, pincer maneuver) so readers can follow actions on the ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report environmental and operational conditions that affected actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe weather, terrain, and other conditions that shaped operations (e.g., "dense fog", "extremely cold weather", "the high central ridge", "fog ... hampered subsequent operations, making air support almost impossible").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how fog, cold, ridges, and other conditions limited or enabled movement, support, target selection and casualty outcomes so the operational narrative includes causal context, not just events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report casualties, captures and material losses with qualifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide numbers or proportions of casualties/captures and equipment losses, but qualify them when sources conflict or may exaggerate (e.g., "killed more than two-thirds of one Japanese force", "captured large quantities of enemy equipment", Japanese claims vs. U.S. statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting casualty figures, include the source and indicate certainty (confirmed, claimed, estimated). Note when opposing sides give differing tallies and avoid presenting contested numbers as uncontested fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain command relationships and inter-service coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify overall command and the interplay of services in an operation (e.g., "over-all campaign is under Navy command, although all the troops ashore on Attu are Army units", "Army is greatly indebted to the Navy for its finely co-ordinated support").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which service or headquarters has overall command, and detail cooperation (naval bombardment facilitating Army landings) to show how joint operations were organized and executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include tactical and technical details of equipment seized or destroyed
rubrics_metrics.description: List captured enemy matériel and destruction counts (e.g., "captured ... an entire anti-aircraft battery with a complete supply", "Flying Fortresses ... destroyed 437 parked planes", "destruction of seventy-three enemy planes").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report specific types and counts of weapons, batteries, ships and aircraft when available. Such details lend concreteness to operational results and indicate the material impact of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations and recorded broadcasts to present voice and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate verbatim quotations from officials, reporters and broadcasts (e.g., quoted broadcast passages describing bombardment, Mr. Stimson's remarks, Japanese reporter assertions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed direct quotes for significant assertions or vivid scenes, and indicate the source and manner of capture (live quote, recorded broadcast, press conference) so readers can assess tone and origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide broader strategic and political context
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect battlefield reports to larger strategy and policy debates (e.g., discussion of Churchill/Eden on bombing strategy, "sea, land and air forces ... welded into a single vision").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Augment action reporting with analysis of implications: how a battle affects campaigns, allied strategy (bombing program), international diplomacy and public morale. Use speeches (Churchill, Eden) and conference comments to illustrate policy direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and report propaganda, morale effects and information control
rubrics_metrics.description: Report signs of enemy propaganda or information withholding and their morale effects (e.g., "Japanese assertions are similar to many Japanese claims in the Pacific war that later were exploded", "Berlin was still withholding details of the damage from the German public", Mosquito operations causing 'mosquito fever').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note when regimes suppress information or when enemy broadcasts are likely intended to influence morale. Explain observable effects on behavior (holding bombers at home) to help readers interpret wartime messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document civilian impact, reprisals and occupation abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Include reports of civilian suffering, executions, reprisals and occupation policies with sources (e.g., "German firing squads have killed 50,000 Frenchmen since the armistice", "400 civilians ... executed in Belgrade", "milk is deliberately poured away and corn in fields is set on fire").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing occupation atrocities or civilian hardships, attribute to named agencies or witnesses, give estimated numbers, and place the incidents within the context of resistance or occupation policy so readers understand scale and cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite expert technical assessments for specialized claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When technical consequences are reported (e.g., dam damage), include expert evaluations (e.g., William Halcrow saying two years probably required to repair the dams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use named experts to interpret technical or long-term effects (engineers on dam repair) rather than leaving readers with vague consequences; include expert credentials where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify air and naval operation results and losses
rubrics_metrics.description: Give counts of aircraft and ships destroyed or lost on both sides and describe the nature of engagements (e.g., "destruction of seventy-three enemy planes ... cost was four Allied aircraft", "twenty-nine planes shot down in dogfights ... forty-four blasted to bits on airfields").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide balanced tallies of enemy losses and friendly losses, indicate where figures come from, and describe combat intensity (dogfights, eight-hour bombardment) to convey scale and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with the most significant facts and summarize key outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Front-load the report with principal outcomes of an engagement (e.g., Americans closed on Japanese from two directions; "over-all campaign is under Navy command"; large numbers of enemy planes destroyed) so readers grasp the main point quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a clear lede that states the central developments. Use subsequent paragraphs to expand with details, attribution, context and analysis so readers obtain both headline facts and supporting evidence.
